utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Egrlic. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you, I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask how much time I have got left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that you will have one hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If I can finish even sooner, I will do so. I will not waste our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask you, Mr. Egrlic, about something you said yesterday on page 19963 responding to my question whether you went to Croatia during the war. It's in line 16 to 20. Whether you visited Croatia during the war, you said you did not do so during the war, and you confirmed that. You said, "As far as I know, I did not." However, in your testimony in the Zupljanin case, which is 65 ter 22085, on page 6810, I will read both question and answer in English so that it would be correctly recorded: [In English] [As read] "Q. And then you speak of an occasion where you travelled to Zagreb, to Croatia, to meet some people from Switzerland, and then you also mentioned Alija Bilic, that you travelled -- that you travelled in your car and that on that occasion you took over 18 Swiss francs. "A. That was the assistance they provided for humanitarian aid. "Q. Did you take that money then to Sarajevo, to the SDA party? Did you turn that money over to those purposes? "A. I didn't." [Interpretation] So you did visit Zagreb during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before you answer, Mr. Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just a clarification on the page numbers. I don't have the page numbers of the Stanisic Zupljanin case extending into the 6800s. Can the accused please check that and indicate whether he misspoke and there's a different page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are they uploaded?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6118.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That clarifies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the question, Mr. Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then please proceed to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for my visit to Zagreb, I said yesterday, as far as I remember, that I did go there. Whether the war was still on-going is something I cannot confirm, because I passed through territories where I did not see that the war was on-going. One was free to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you oppose the deployment of some parts of the Knin Corps on Laniste?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the time when Bosnia was still an integral part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was at some point in early 1992, as far as I remember. In the month of February, when even though some people opposed that and others were in favour of that, a part of the Knin Corps did arrive in Laniste.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement from 1997, in 65 ter 22083, on page 5, described that members of the Assembly, I suppose the Kljuc Assembly, those who were Bosnians, opposed the idea, but they were the minority. Would you agree with me that no army in the world, including the JNA, would not ask for approval from the local authorities to deploy troops in the territory?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have asked me a question which was raised at the meeting of the Council for National Defence. It shouldn't have been on the agenda, because there was no discussion about it. However, the outcome of the vote was such as it was, because the Bosniaks who were opposed to the idea were out-voted and the army came there. We believed that there was no need to station parts of the Knin Corps in that area, in particular not in the Laniste area, which is a forest area where some labour was performed by workers from a forestry company. They had some of their premises there, their restaurant and offices, a small repair facility, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you wish to say that the president of the municipality Jovo Banjac, who was also the president of the National Defence council as part of his responsibilities, included this issue in the agenda even though he did not have to do that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he had to do it, but he did include it in the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was he aware of the position of the Muslim community in Kljuc, and was that the reason for him to include it in the agenda?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stated our positions in an open manner. Even at that session we said that we opposed the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same statement, on page 5 in B/C/S, probably in English as well, that's 22083, you said that you went to Laniste to see what was happening, and you said "I saw cannons with barrels turned towards the town of Kljuc. They were dug in." And is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation, why would the JNA turn its cannons towards the town of Kljuc in which the Serbs are the majority population and they also held power in that town?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to know that too, why they came there and why they came with guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it's not logical, is it, that from the fact that the barrels of the guns were turned in some direction you would draw such a conclusion; the barrels have to be turned in some direction, don't they?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From the fact that they were turned towards the town of Kljuc you drew the conclusion that this was a threat for the town?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, later on it really came to happen. It's a fact. The town of Kljuc was -- sustained some damage by the -- from the army which was stationed there and the police which was in the town, so my suspicions proved to be right. A major crime was committed there. The army, the reservists, and the police did that. So it's superfluous to ask such questions, because a barracks was formed there and civilians who had been killed in Biljane were driven through there and then they were thrown in Bezdan. It means that the army participated in the commission of the crime, and I think that there can be no justification. The army was there and it turned out that crimes were really committed under the control of the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, what I'm asking you now is about the following fact: Were the Serbs the majority population in Kljuc, and did they hold power in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you look at the data from the census, they were not the majority. Bosniaks, Yugoslavs, and others made up more than one-half of the population in Kljuc. But it is a fact that the Serbs won the elections and they were in power. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And these elections held in 1990, were they also a kind of census?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the census was conducted in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if the Serbs and the Serbian Democratic Party won the election, then it's clear to you that those Yugoslavs you mentioned were for the most part also Serbs, which additionally increases the number of Serbs in the general population; correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean to say by that. Can you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you place the Yugoslavs together with the Muslim and the Croatian block as if the Yugoslavs were not for the most part Serbs or as if the Yugoslavs were against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just talking about the census, not about who was in favour of what. Some people declare themselves as Yugoslavs and then it turned out later on that the Bosniaks were those who, for the most part, declared themselves as such. But there were others as well; there were a few Serbs and Croats who also declared themselves in the like manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us not dwell on this topic. Mr. Egrlic, you are now saying that in 1991 the Muslims, for the most part, were in favour of Yugoslavia, at the moment when they had already decided to leave Yugoslavia. What I say is that in 1991 when the census was conducted neither the Muslims nor the Croats declared themselves as Yugoslavs because they had decided to leave Yugoslavia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about a part of the population, the people who declare themselves as Yugoslavs by ethnicity. We have talked about this. Let us try to avoid confusion. The Bosniaks declare themselves as Bosniaks, but there were some people who declared themselves in terms of ethnicity as Yugoslavs. And there is nothing in dispute about that, because there was a special category in the census as Yugoslavs, and you can see the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that moment, the JNA, the part of the Knin Corps, was also predominantly Serb, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why would the predominantly Serb JNA turn its guns towards the predominantly Serb populated Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you should best ask the commander who did turn the barrels in that direction why he did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you active in your party during the war, once you had been exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the function that you performed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the president of the Municipal Board, but that was as a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you join the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But I was a member of the War Presidency of the Kljuc municipality which was in refuge and its seat was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Zenica and Travnik, did you cooperate with the War Presidency of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I met everyone, the representatives of all the municipalities which were exiled to the area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And what was the duty of the War Presidencies which were in exile in Zenica or in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their duty was to take care of the population in the sense of providing humanitarian assistance and resolving problems which arose among the exiled population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you welcome people who were leaving Kljuc? For example, if someone left Kljuc and if a bus of the inhabitants arrived, who would take care of them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, once I got there, everybody had been expelled from Kljuc already, so no one arrived anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please refrain from using such qualifications and say that they were expellees. We established yesterday that one needed ten or 15 documents or forms. They were refugees. They had fled, rather than expellees. They were not expelled. You are putting me in a position where we have to clarify this all over again.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were really expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I think the witness has addressed the issue, I simply wanted to point out the Court has previously discouraged the accused from attempting to qualify or limit the witness's responses, and I think that was another example, should be -- it should not take place and should be discouraged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Please bear that in mind, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But I think that I have a right to warn the witness not to make any qualifications, because we both reached a conclusion that they themselves wanted to go. They were not forced to go by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, when you ask a question of somebody in cross-examination, you are open to whatever answer that the witness thinks is appropriate. It's one of the dangers of cross-examination. That means, that's why you have to be very focused and specific in your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I may add, Mr. President and Your Honour: That is an absolutely false representation of what the witness said and the alleged agreement between the accused and the witness with regard to the voluntariness of the departure of people from Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: And, Mr. Karadzic, may I say this: If the witness gives you an answer with which you don't agree, put to him that you don't agree with this and, if you care to, put to him what exactly is your case on this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was under the impression that I had done that, but obviously I didn't do it in a skillful manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you repeat yesterday what you spoke about on several occasions before, that you were in favour of reaching a consensus among the ethnic communities in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that also the position of your party all over Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now briefly look at 1D4432.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this document? This is intended for the media and it reflects the position of the SDA concerning the Vienna Agreement on the formation of the Croat/Muslim Federation. Please look at the fifth paragraph, where it says: "The Muslim people should trust the decision taken by President Izetbegovic. There is no reason for concern. The SDA has absolute majority in the Assembly of BH, and the Assembly according to the constitution of the Federation has general control over the operation of the government and the army." Therefore, do you agree that the position of the SDA was that only such agreements should be accepted that would guarantee them that they would exert complete and full control?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time, and I have no comment. I'm really reluctant to comment on something that I never saw before. I have no detailed knowledge about this, and I don't want to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But this is the position of your party. And you said that their view was that the [indiscernible] should work on the principle of a consensus. Does this indicate that a consensus was going to be reached, or is somebody's going to take predominance?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to draw any conclusions of the sort. This speaks about some kind of agreement between the Bosniaks and the Croats, whereas what kind of position was taken vis-à-vis the Serbs and other ethnicities, there's no mention of that. Therefore, one cannot conclude that the party was opposed to reaching an agreement with the others, and I don't think that you are right in claiming that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that this paragraph indicates that they should accept this because they have managed to have the majority?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, Your Honours, that I honestly cannot express any opinions about something that I see for the first time. I don't know anything about it. This was taken out of a certain context, I suppose, and therefore I'm not able to construe any announcement made by the party. All I can do is to comment and to interpret the things that I myself wrote and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence. Let's look at the document so that we can see the date. Can we zoom out. The date is the 12th of May, and this press release was passed on to all the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you do not object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1750, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Egrlic, we agreed that you knew the locations where exhumations were carried out but that you didn't know where and how those people were killed among other things due to the fact that you had already been in captivity.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended all the exhumations and I saw everything with my own eyes; however, I was not at the site where people perished. All I know about that comes from the stories that I heard from other people who experienced them themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was the duty of the civilian protection to carry out the "asanacija" or the hygenic measures on a battle-field?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly look at P3316.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It refers to the neighbouring town of Sanski Most. We have a similar paper for Kljuc, only we have to find it first. Do you see here that the municipal staff of the civilian protection issued an order to carry out "asanacija" including the finding and the burial of the bodies at a designated location; is that correct? And Mico [as interpreted] Kljujic, obviously a Croat, was charged with this task. This is obviously a Croat surname. Do you know that whenever there's a war, once the fighting starts, it is customary for the civilian protection to come out to find the bodies and to mark these locations so that people can be easily found later on?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And to lower them onto the trucks and load them off into caves, is that the way how you perform assanation [as interpreted]? There was quite a few people who were killed in that way and thrown into the caves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that in all areas people who were killed in one location were buried in different locations?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Sanski Most. I also know that there were caves there as well and people were collected and their bodies thrown into them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the fighting, do you know how many Serbs were killed and how many Muslims were killed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know these figures. I know what figures were printed in the media. Some say they were correct, some say they were wrong. Unfortunately there is no official document as yet on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Kljuc Light Brigade sustained losses in terms of 300 members were killed and 17 were wounded?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many people were killed. I'm talking here about the civilians who were killed, who were later exhumed, and that they were buried at the cemeteries with dignity. One can always go and take a look at that, and if you don't believe anyone, you can count those headstone, and it is really a horrendous sight. Everyone who comes there for a first time has goose bumps once he sees the situation. I don't know if you yourself had an opportunity to see that, but you have these kind of cemeteries all across Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm not disputing that both the Serbs and the Croats and other ethnicities were killed, but the plight of the civilians, the fact that they were taken out from their houses and shot dead, that happened to the Bosniaks of Kljuc. You can imagine how big the figure of 600 people is when you have them attending a football game, let alone when you kill so many people. In addition, 3.500 Bosniak houses were destroyed. A number of mosques were destroyed. 17.000 people were made to leave. So they became virtually extinct. So what are we talking here about? We are talking about some pieces of paper. This is shameful. And I really don't want to look at any papers coming from Sanski Most. Mr. Karadzic, there is no justification for this kind of crime, no matter how hard you try to disprove that by presenting certain papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself see any of the killings?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other people saw them. I believed them. I saw bodies being exhumed. All of that I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since you asked me, I can tell you that I attended a lot of exhumations and mass burials. But I'm asking you: Do you know and can you testify to the fact of the exact location where those people were killed and how? Did you see that with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's answered. Please move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 1104.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Meanwhile, Mr. Witness, is it correct that between the 27th through to 31st of May the assistant police commander was killed, a number of soldiers were captured, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were the president of the Kljuc government. Yesterday I received information that this convoy that came under attack had been announced, had proper markings, and had an escort, and nobody from the convoy opened fire, however fire was opened from Velagici on the bus and as a result a number of soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't witness this event, and I did not participate in the work of municipal organs from 7th May onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, on the 1st of June, a crime was committed in Velagici where the civilians whose headstones you showed us were killed. Now, this is an Official Note about this location. Without trying to make any excuses for this kind of revenge, Mr. Egrlic, can you agree that 1st of June is after the 31st of May and that the sequence of events of these tragic and unacceptable events was that Velagici first fired at the convoy and after that somebody came to take revenge by slaughtering the civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think, in the guise of trying to clarify a sequence which is already clear, the accused is embedding representations about the state of the evidence which are inaccurate and to which the witness has already testified to the contrary. So that question has to be either rephrased, deconstructed, or abandoned, but it's an unfair attempt to get the witness to affirm something in one context, when he's already indicated the contrary earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please make question simple and direct, otherwise you'll not be benefitted from the answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Egrlic, did you know that this case was investigated, that already on the 3rd of June a commission visited the site and recorded it as one can see from this Official Note?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't get the interpretation. Could you kindly repeat your answer, Mr. Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regard this previous question, I said that I didn't know anything about that because I was arrested on the 28th of May. And after that date I don't know anything about what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1751, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, do you know that upon entering Kljuc in 1995 you discovered a lot of investigation material which served as a basis for trying a large number of Serb perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with that. I was never involved in any kind of work dealing with such materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you if you agree that even in late May the Serbian side expressed understanding and delayed their demands for weapons to be surrendered, hoping that there would be a calming and reconciliation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that an ultimatum was issued that was broadcast on Radio Kljuc. And the ultimatum said that weapons had to be surrendered until a certain dead-line, I believe it was the 14th, otherwise weapons will be seized with all means available. I know that was said on the radio, and I can reproduce it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that dead-line postponed a number of times upon the request of the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that. I was not involved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us take a look at D1728.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The sharpest crisis involving weapons began on the 31st of May, after that you were wounded and people visited you in hospital. And Mr. Omer Filipovic -- take a look at the first sentence: [As read] "Since Mr. Omer Filipovic on behalf of the Muslims and all the people who possess weapons has asked for postponement of dead-line until 1000 hours on 29 May, and the Kljuc -- and a token of understanding for this proposal, the Kljuc Defence command has accepted his proposal under the condition of the seven captured soldiers from the Crljeni area and the assistant commander of the police station in Kljuc will be handed over by 1700 hours." So you see that by that time they had not been handed over and the Serbian side accepted the postponement of the dead-line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered. I don't believe you should pressurise me if it was this way or not. I was not involved in the events, and I don't know. I can see what it reads. But whether it was that way or not isn't anything I could know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you are unfamiliar with many things that happened after 28 of May, I will conclude this cross-examination. Thank you. And please don't feel that I'm attacking you, which I'm not doing. I'm only looking for the truth, but truth is not easy to find. And you can be sure that I have the same position toward the war. We could have done everything much better without the war, and that was an option that was open to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was just rising to object to the continuation of the concluding commentary, but it stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You don't have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Egrlic. On behalf of this Chamber, my colleagues, and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague yet again, notwithstanding all the difficult situations, to give it. Now you are free to go. Thank you very much. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I take it that we exhausted the witnesses for this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any matters to raise? There's one thing the Chamber wants to clarify. Mr. Tieger, yesterday you filed a Prosecution motion to convert the mode of evidentiary admission for one witness and notification that two witnesses will be called during the Srebrenica component of the case. In the request, the Prosecution asks to convert the mode of evidentiary admission of -- admission for Mirsad Malagic from Rule 92 bis to Rule 92 ter. I note that on 21st of December, 2009, the Chamber already admitted the evidence of this witness pursuant to Rule 92 bis without requiring that she appears for cross-examination. The Chamber would be benefitted, Mr. Tieger, before hearing from the Defence, if the Prosecution could explain what its request entails. In paragraph 4, the Prosecution states that it -- I quote: "It would be in the interest of justice for the Chamber to hear this witness live." However, your request is that she be converted to a Rule 92 ter witness. Could you please explain the scope of your request and how you would expect the testimony of this witness to proceed if your request was granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe the Court has had ample experience with the process of a partial 92 ter and even full 92 ter submissions, so I think the reference to live testimony there is a reflection not of the -- of the balance of written evidence versus oral presentation but the sheer -- the difference between no oral presentation by the witness or viva voce presentation by the witness at all. And the witness's presence in court, in short, the witness [sic] gets to see and hear the witness to some extent, notwithstanding the presentation or submission of large portions of her evidence through the submission of the 92 ter package. So it's, again, an appropriate balance being struck that provides the Court in this instance with an opportunity to see and hear the witness, which will be in the interest of justice. So we didn't mean to suggest by use of the term "live" that there would be an abrogation or elimination of the benefits of 92 ter. Simply that in this instance it afforded advantages that the straight 92 bis submission did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To use the ICTY jargon, if witness's evidence is to be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter, I mean full ter, there's no difference on the part of the Prosecution. So I take it that you are requesting to lead some part of that witness's evidence live, i.e., the evidence is to be admitted in part pursuant to partial Rule 92 ter, so I wanted you to indicate what part you are going to lead live.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as I sit here at the moment, I mean, if that's the submission the Court wants us to make, we're prepared to do so, Mr. President, and identify with some greater specificity those particular portions. As the Court has seen in the past, the Prosecution's practice has, in partial 92 ter circumstances, has generally been to focus on areas that might benefit from further clarification or illumination or the most salient parts of the witness's evidence, but I know you want something specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm asking this witness in this case. The witness's evidence has been already admitted, so we, the Chamber, wants to know the reason behind it, what part of the evidence is to be led live.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, that's understood, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then unless there's any other matter, the hearing is now adjourned. And we'll resume on the 18th of October, at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of October, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 9.51 a.m.,
